html:
Hernando de Soto was a Spanish conquistador who led the first European army deep into what is now the south-eastern United States, from 1539 to 1543. He was the first European known to have crossed the Mississippi River.

He first made his name and fortune in Central America and then in Peru, where he rode with Francisco Pizarro in the conquest of the Inca Empire and met Atahualpa at Cajamarca. Rich from Inca gold, he got a royal licence to conquer Florida.

In 1539 he landed near Tampa Bay with some 600 men, horses and pigs. For four years the army wandered through Florida, Georgia, the Carolinas, Tennessee, Alabama, Mississippi and Arkansas, looking for gold. They wintered with the Apalachee, fought a bloody battle at Mabila, and seized food and porters from towns of the Mississippian world, among the ancestors of the Cherokee, Creek, Chickasaw and Choctaw. They found no gold.

De Soto died of fever on the banks of the Mississippi in 1542, and his men sank his body in the river. The survivors, about half the army, built boats and escaped to Mexico in 1543. Their accounts, and the later history by Inca Garcilaso de la Vega, are among the few pictures of these chiefdoms before European diseases, perhaps spread partly by the expedition itself, broke many of them apart.
